inf3-storage-raid.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. If every hard drive will fail, what keeps your family's photos safe? Two different things working together. RAID keeps the box running when one drive dies. A real backup, an independent copy kept somewhere else and actually test-restored, protects against everything RAID cannot: deletion, ransomware, fire and theft.
inf3-storage-raid.example: TWO BAD DAYS. Say one drive dies on a Tuesday. RAID keeps the NAS running; you confirm the backup is current, swap the dead drive, and the array rebuilds. Now say a folder of photos is deleted by mistake, or a fire takes the house. RAID cannot help with either. The independent backup can: the encrypted copy sealed on the church NAS, the one you have already proven by a test restore.
inf3-storage-raid.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What keeps your family's photos safe when drives fail? Not one drive, and not RAID alone. RAID carries you through a dead drive; a backup carries you through everything else. Keep three copies, on two kinds of media, with one offsite, and restore from it on purpose so it is proof, not a hope. Then the failure of any single drive is routine, not loss. Knowing the state of what you hold and protecting it is wisdom, not fear (Proverbs 27:23).

teen.open: Every hard drive dies someday. What keeps the photos safe? RAID keeps things running when one drive breaks, and a real backup somewhere else saves you from everything else.
teen.close: So it's two things: RAID for a dead drive, and a tested backup for deletions, fires and theft. A backup you've never restored is only a hope.

senior.open: Since every drive will fail, safety rests on two separate provisions: RAID, which keeps the system running through a single drive failure, and an independent, tested backup kept offsite.
senior.close: So the title is answered. RAID and a proven offsite backup together keep the family's photos safe, and the 3-2-1 rule with a real test restore turns a failure into a routine repair.

inf4-network-gateway.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who gets to walk through your front door, and who stays in their own room? The gateway decides both. As the door, its firewall keeps out what should not come in. As the walls, it splits one network into separate rooms called VLANs, so the family, the church, the clinic and the rentals each stay in their own, walled off from the others.
inf4-network-gateway.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who walks through the door, and who stays in their own room? Only what the firewall lets in comes through the front door. Inside, each group has its own VLAN: the family, COLG, the clinic with its health-privacy rules, the rentals. A contractor or tenant comes in by the gateway's own WireGuard, not onto the family's private network, and RADIUS gives each person one set of credentials matched to their role. Walls and a watch, like Nehemiah's, and every wall documented so it can be trusted.

inf7-gpu-vram-farm.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why does a 70B AI model need about 48 GB of GPU memory? Because the model's weights, the billions of numbers it learned, have to fit inside the graphics card's own memory, called VRAM, to run. A small model fits in a little. A 70-billion-parameter model at common compression needs roughly 48 GB to hold.
inf7-gpu-vram-farm.example: SIZING THE FARM. The plan in this lesson reaches that number honestly: two used RTX 3090 cards together give 48 GB of VRAM, enough to hold a 70B-class model, in a chassis sized to add a third card for 72 GB. The cost is around $5,000, plus a separate church node. The lesson counts that cost against sovereignty, capability and data control, not against a small monthly API bill.
inf7-gpu-vram-farm.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does a 70B model need about 48 GB? Because the GPU's thousands of small cores can only do their parallel work on weights that fit in its VRAM, and a 70-billion-parameter model at common compression takes roughly 48 GB of it. That one number gates everything. It is why the NAS, with no graphics card, cannot do this work, and why the farm is planned around 48 GB. Know your tools and size them honestly, counting the cost first (Luke 14:28).

teen.open: Why does a huge AI model need so much memory? Its learned numbers have to fit inside the graphics card's own memory, called VRAM. A 70B model needs about 48 GB.
teen.close: So the memory number decides everything. If the model doesn't fit in VRAM, it can't run there. That's why the plan is built around 48 GB.

senior.open: A 70-billion-parameter model needs roughly 48 GB because its weights must fit within the GPU's own memory, VRAM, before the card's parallel cores can run it.

inf9-keeping-it-alive.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who notices first when your system breaks? The system itself should, before any person goes looking. Every workflow carries a health check, failures are caught instead of hidden, and ntfy pushes an alert to your phone, with a failure pushed at high priority. What stops it from running away is three brakes: a budget ceiling, a single-instance lock, and a kill-switch, with the automation shipped turned off. Here is how it fits together.
inf9-keeping-it-alive.example: ONE STUCK JOB. Say a timed job hangs in the middle of the night. Its health check catches the failure, and ntfy pushes it to your phone at high priority, so you hear before anyone goes looking. When the timer fires again, the single-instance lock sees the stuck run and does not pile a second one on top. If it keeps going, the budget ceiling stops it, and the kill-switch pauses it instead of letting it charge ahead.
inf9-keeping-it-alive.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who notices first when your system breaks? Not a person who happened to check. The system watches itself, catches its own failures, and tells your phone through ntfy, while the in-app inventory honestly says "not connected" or "stale" instead of a comforting number. And what stops it from running away is the three brakes: a budget ceiling, a lock that keeps a new run off a stuck one, and a kill-switch that pauses on overrun, all shipped off until someone is watching. That is the faithful manager keeping watch day and night (Luke 12:42; Nehemiah 4:9).

teen.open: Who finds out first when something breaks? The system should, by sending an alert straight to your phone.
teen.close: So the system tells you first, through health checks and alerts. And three brakes, a budget, a lock, and a kill-switch, keep any automation from running away.

senior.open: The title asks who notices first when a system fails, and what keeps it from running away. The answer is that the system watches itself and reports, and that every self-running automation carries three brakes.
senior.close: So the answer is twofold. The system notices first and pushes the alert to your phone, and a budget ceiling, a single-instance lock, and a kill-switch keep any automation from running away. That is faithful watching, day and night.

inf10-build-right-raise-builders.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can you teach it? That is the test. You truly own a part of the stack, home or church, when you can write its simple checklist or record its sequence and explain it to one other person. A build that lives only in one person's memory is lucky, not mature. Here is why the Word ties owning to teaching.
inf10-build-right-raise-builders.example: ONE PART, ONE PERSON. Say the part you understand best is the broadcast start-up sequence. You write its simple checklist, or record yourself running it, step by step. Then you walk one other person through it until they can run it without you. Now that part no longer rides on your memory, someone new can operate it, and you have passed the test this lesson sets.
inf10-build-right-raise-builders.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can you teach it? If you can, you own it. The lesson gave two marks of a mature build: reliability, written down in checklists and SOPs so nothing rides on one memory, and multiplication, entrusting it to faithful people who will be able to teach others also (2 Timothy 2:2). So pick your part, write it plain, and teach one person, heartily, as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23). Then the build, and the calling under it, outlasts you.
